opening.say: Here's a funny thing about blue jeans. The dye that colors them is a pale, yellowish green when it's dissolved in water.
The blue shows up only afterward, once the dyed cloth comes out of the vat and meets the open air.
So something happens in those first seconds out of the bath, and that's the whole trick we're about to look at.

more.say: Indigo on its own won't dissolve in water. It's a stubborn blue powder, so dyers had to coax it into a different form first.
They added something that steals oxygen, which turns the powder into a form that dissolves, and that form is the pale yellow green one.
Cotton soaks up that dissolved form easily. At that point the thread looks yellow green, and nothing blue is on it yet.

plan.setup: Watch one thread as it leaves the vat.
plan.narration: [[thread-dips]]Dip a thread into the vat and it soaks up the pale, dissolved indigo. [[lift-out]]Lift it out, and oxygen in the air gets to work. [[color-shift]]Within seconds the thread turns green, then blue. [[locked-in]]The dye turns back into its insoluble form, stuck inside the fibers. [[repeat-dips]]That's why dyers dip again and again, and why jeans fade slowly.
plan.plan:
thread-dips: a white cotton thread lowers into a vat of pale yellow green liquid and takes on that color.
lift-out: the thread rises into the air, small oxygen molecules labeled O2 drift toward it.
color-shift: the thread color fades from yellow green through green to deep blue as the oxygen touches it.
locked-in: zoom into a fiber, showing dissolved dye molecules becoming larger blue clumps trapped in the fiber.
repeat-dips: the same thread dips several more times, each pass making the blue visibly darker.
plan.close: Why might the blue sit mostly on the outside of each thread?
